defaults.permitted_development: Across Northumberland, a modest rooflight is usually on the simpler planning route if it sits close to the roof slope, does not exceed the existing ridge and avoids creating a problematic side-facing opening. That fallback can disappear where an Article 4 direction or an old planning condition has removed the normal householder right.

rules.height_rules: Across Northumberland, the main dimensional test is how closely the rooflight follows the existing roof slope and whether it remains below the ridge.
rules.depth_rules: Across Northumberland, bulky or heavily projecting rooflight designs may fall outside the ordinary householder route.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Northumberland, side-facing roof windows should be obscure-glazed. Opening parts should normally be kept at least 1.7 metres above the floor of the room served.
rules.roof_rules: Across Northumberland, flush or low-profile units generally sit comfortably within the category of a roof alteration, while bulkier structures begin to resemble dormers or other roof additions.
rules.materials_rules: Across Northumberland, choose a rooflight and flashing detail that look integrated with the roof rather than bolted on. Low-profile frames and restrained external finishes are usually easiest to justify.

restrictions.conservation_area: Roof-lights on prominent roof slopes in conservation areas often face a closer design review, especially where they would affect a traditional roofscape or visible frontage.
restrictions.listed_building: Roof-lights in listed buildings are commonly treated as heritage works because the roof covering, structure and external appearance all contribute to significance.
restrictions.article4_notes: Roof-specific planning conditions and Article 4 directions are a common reason why an otherwise modest roof-light still needs planning permission.
